subject: Climate & Environment
title: Parks and Mental Health
description: One-minute skill: Parks and Mental Health.

hook.text: People who live near green spaces have lower rates of depression, anxiety, and heart disease.

buildup.text: Even 20 minutes in a park reduces stress hormones and lowers blood pressure measurably.

discovery.text: Japan calls it shinrin-yoku — forest bathing. The science confirms that trees heal.

twist.text: Low-income neighborhoods have far fewer parks and trees than wealthy ones — a green gap.

climax.text: Cities that invest in green space see returns in public health, property values, and social cohesion.

punchline.text: A park isn't a luxury. It's infrastructure for human well-being.

quiz.question: How quickly can spending time in a park reduce stress hormones?

details.summary: Urban parks and green spaces provide significant mental health benefits, reducing stress, anxiety, and depression. Studies show that people living near green spaces have lower rates of mental illness and that even brief exposure to nature lowers cortisol levels and blood pressure.
details.whyItMatters: As urban populations grow and mental health challenges rise, accessible green space is a cost-effective public health intervention that also supports climate resilience.
takeaways: Proximity to green space reduces stress and anxiety
Even brief nature exposure lowers cortisol and blood pressure
Equitable green access is a public health priority

faq.question: How much green space do people need for health benefits?
faq.answer: Research suggests that 120 minutes per week in nature significantly improves health and well-being. The World Health Organization recommends that all residents live within 300 meters of green space. Even small pocket parks provide measurable benefits.

faq.question: Is green space equitably distributed in cities?
faq.answer: No. Low-income and minority neighborhoods consistently have less tree canopy and fewer parks. This green gap worsens heat exposure, air pollution, and health disparities. Many cities now prioritize greening underserved neighborhoods to address environmental justice.
